question: What special mask is a must-have for Airborne Precautions?

options.A: Disposable plastic apron
options.B: Clean non-sterile gloves
options.C: Standard surgical mask
options.D: N95 respirator mask

explanation: Tiny germs floating in the air need an N95 respirator to filter them out before they reach your lungs. Safety first!

question: A patient comes to the clinic with severe belly pain and rectal bleeding after using a local herbal enema. What is the biggest nursing concern here?

options.A: Severe allergic rhinitis and upper airway swelling
options.B: Sudden complete obstruction of the upper esophagus
options.C: Trauma to the rectal mucosa and systemic toxicity
options.D: Immediate development of peripheral neuropathy

explanation: Harsh local enemas can easily tear the delicate lining of the rectum and quickly push strong, unmeasured chemicals straight into the bloodstream. Ouch! Patient safety is key here.

question: Which mental health challenge is very common among young brides who are cut off from their friends?

options.A: Bipolar manic episodes
options.B: Schizophrenic hallucinations
options.C: Depression and anxiety
options.D: Obsessive compulsive rituals

explanation: Loneliness, losing their childhood, and heavy adult responsibilities often trigger deep depression and anxiety in young wives.

question: Why is having clear rules for DRF exemptions so important for hospital staff?

options.A: It stops staff from showing personal bias when giving out free drugs
options.B: It allows the pharmacy to increase drug prices for wealthy patients
options.C: It ensures that doctors do not have to write any medical prescriptions
options.D: It guarantees that the federal government will pay the hospital bonus funds

explanation: Clear criteria remove guesswork and favoritism, making sure that only genuinely qualified patients receive free medications.

question: How do immune-based idiosyncratic reactions differ from quick, everyday drug allergies?

options.A: They never cause any visible skin rashes or external symptoms.
options.B: They often take days or weeks of exposure to develop fully.
options.C: They only occur when a patient takes a liquid form of medication.
options.D: They disappear quickly even if the patient continues taking the drug.

explanation: Unlike a sudden allergy that flares up immediately, immune-based idiosyncrasies usually need a little time—days or weeks—to build up before you see a reaction.

question: Which of these common chest tube practices is actually dangerous and should be avoided?

options.A: Checking breath sounds and respiratory status every four hours
options.B: Clamping the chest tube continuously for routine nursing tasks
options.C: Taping all tubing connections securely to prevent air leaks
options.D: Keeping the drainage system upright and below chest level

explanation: Great clinical thinking! Never clamp a chest tube routinely; it traps air and fluid inside, which can quickly turn into a life-threatening tension pneumothorax.

question: What is the main job of a standard hearing aid?

options.A: To amplify surrounding sounds so the damaged ear can detect them
options.B: To convert spoken words directly into written text on a screen
options.C: To remove impacted earwax from deep inside the ear canal
options.D: To surgically replace the cochlea with an electronic processor

explanation: Exactly! Think of a hearing aid as a tiny personal amplifier that makes everyday sounds loud enough for the ear to pick up.

question: How does chronic high blood pressure eventually lead to heart failure?

options.A: It forces the left ventricle to work so hard that the muscle thickens and weakens over time.
options.B: It fills the heart chambers with excess air.
options.C: It shrinks the heart valves until they fall apart.
options.D: It causes the heart to stop beating entirely within a few hours.

explanation: Constantly pumping against high resistance makes the heart muscle enlarge and eventually lose its pumping efficiency, resulting in heart failure. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T16#GNS324_U4_T16_h7)

question: When is the best time to start a chosen birth control method after an abortion?

options.A: Only after the six-week follow-up visit
options.B: On the exact same day as the abortion procedure
options.C: After waiting for three complete menstrual cycles
options.D: When cervical mucus changes appear

explanation: Starting contraception on day one ensures the patient is protected before ovulation sneaks up on them.

question: What is the primary function of vitamins in the human body?

options.A: Building thick outer walls around every body cell
options.B: Storing excess fat inside the abdominal cavity
options.C: Supplying the majority of daily caloric energy
options.D: Acting as coenzymes to regulate metabolic pathways

explanation: Vitamins do not provide calories, but they work as coenzymes to help chemical reactions run smoothly in the body. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T015#GNS227_U2_T015_h3)

question: Why are clients told to avoid caffeine before doing a cardiac stress test?

options.A: Caffeine lowers blood pressure to dangerous levels
options.B: Caffeine makes the ECG machine run out of paper faster
options.C: Caffeine can artificially speed up the heart rate and interfere with test findings
options.D: Caffeine causes severe stomach cramps during exercise

explanation: That's right! Stimulants like coffee or tea affect heart rhythm, making it tough to measure how the heart truly responds to exercise.

question: Why are most biotechnology-derived drugs given by injection instead of as a pill?

options.A: Oral pills taste too bitter for patients to swallow safely
options.B: Liquid biotechnology drugs cannot fit inside a standard capsule
options.C: Stomach acid and digestive enzymes would destroy the protein
options.D: Injections allow the drug to bypass the liver completely forever

explanation: Biotech drugs are made of delicate proteins. If swallowed, your stomach acid would digest them before they could do their job!

question: Why is it important for a nurse to understand a patient's cultural background regarding death and grief?

options.A: Grief customs and expressions vary greatly across different cultures
options.B: Cultural practices are the only factor that influences healing
options.C: All cultures follow the exact same five stages of grief
options.D: Hospital policy requires every patient to have a religious burial

explanation: Culture dictates how people mourn, and understanding this helps nurses provide respectful, personalized support. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T8#GNS321_U4_T8_h7)

question: What is the biggest danger of pouring leftover chemicals into empty beverage bottles?

options.A: The chemical instantly turns into a harmless gas
options.B: Labels become permanently stamped into the plastic
options.C: People may accidentally drink the toxic chemical
options.D: The plastic material dissolves within a few hours

explanation: You got it! Putting chemicals in drink bottles is a recipe for disaster because it tricks anyone—especially thirsty children—into thinking it's safe juice or water.

question: What is the main trigger that causes blood vessels in the newborn lungs to relax and open?

options.A: Gravity pulling fluid downward
options.B: The sudden release of adrenal hormones
options.C: The physical drop in environmental temperature
options.D: Exposure to oxygen from the first breath

explanation: Oxygen is a powerful natural vasodilator; when air enters the lungs, the sudden oxygen increase relaxes the pulmonary blood vessels. [learn more](GNS121_U6_T9#GNS121_U6_T9_h3)

question: Which feature is most characteristic of a quantitative research study?

options.A: Statistical analysis and measurement
options.B: Detailed personal stories and interviews
options.C: Focus only on historical events
options.D: Absence of any numerical data

explanation: Quantitative research deals with numbers, variables, and measurable outcomes to test hypotheses. [learn more](GNS224_U4_T4#GNS224_U4_T4_h4)

question: In a primary hyposecretion problem, what do you expect the brain's tropic hormone levels to do?

options.A: Zero, because the hypothalamus has completely shut down
options.B: Low, because the brain also stops producing signals
options.C: Normal, because the brain is unaware of the problem
options.D: High, because the brain tries hard to stimulate the lazy gland

explanation: The brain notices the target gland isn't doing its job, so the pituitary keeps shouting louder (making more tropic hormones) to try and wake it up!

question: In family planning clinics, how do we define a 'new acceptor'?

options.A: A nurse newly transferred to manage the reproductive health unit
options.B: A patient returning to the clinic for a routine resupply visit
options.C: A client adopting a modern contraceptive method for the first time
options.D: A community leader who just agreed to support safe motherhood

explanation: Spot on! A new acceptor is simply someone starting modern contraception for the very first time in their life.

question: How do nurses help fulfill a hospitalized patient's need for emotional safety?

options.A: By limiting visits from family members completely
options.B: By performing procedures quickly without warning
options.C: By keeping information about treatments a secret
options.D: By explaining procedures clearly and answering questions honestly

explanation: Clear communication reduces anxiety and helps patients feel secure and in control of their situation. [learn more](GNS112_U1_T4#GNS112_U1_T4_h4)

question: A nurse notices a 16-year-old girl repeatedly visiting the clinic for minor injuries with vague explanations. What should the nurse do first?

options.A: Scold the patient for being clumsy and failing to take proper precautions
options.B: Report the parents immediately to law enforcement without talking to the teen
options.C: Conduct a private psychosocial assessment using a structured tool like HEADSS
options.D: Discharge the patient quickly so other acute emergency cases can be seen

explanation: Correct! Repeated, unexplained injuries are a major red flag. A private, gentle interview using a tool like HEADSS helps uncover abuse or emotional distress.

question: Which organ does the heavy lifting when it comes to adjusting and managing your daily fluid loss?

options.A: Lungs
options.B: Skin
options.C: Liver
options.D: Kidneys

explanation: Spot on! The kidneys are the ultimate fluid supervisors, tweaking how much water leaves your body every single day through urine.

question: Why is it important to check the medication label three times before instilling drops?

options.A: To follow hospital rules without any clear medical purpose
options.B: To catch any potential mistakes and ensure the right drug and dose are given
options.C: To make sure the expiration date is at least five years away
options.D: To help the patient memorize the name of their prescription

explanation: Triple-checking the label is a core safety habit that prevents giving the wrong medication or dose to a patient. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T10#GNS122_U1_T10_h4)

question: What is the term for long-term liver damage caused by repeated inflammation and severe scarring?

options.A: Cholelithiasis
options.B: Steatosis
options.C: Cirrhosis
options.D: Necrosis

explanation: You're doing great! Over time, constant scarring replaces healthy liver tissue with tough fibrous tissue. We call this condition cirrhosis.

question: Why does the body's immune system attack mismatched blood?

options.A: It tries to repair the damaged cells using white blood cells
options.B: It recognizes the foreign antigens as nonself and makes antibodies
options.C: It runs out of normal plasma proteins to handle the extra fluid
options.D: It mistakes the red blood cells for harmful bacteria

explanation: You've got this! The immune system's main job is spotting foreign invaders. When it sees unfamiliar antigens on donated red blood cells, it treats them as dangerous and attacks. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T2#GNS111_U2_T2_h1)

question: An unconscious patient is brought to the ward. After checking their airway and breathing, which scale should you use to assess their brain function and alertness?

options.A: Glasgow Coma Scale
options.B: Sphygmomanometer
options.C: Body mass index chart
options.D: Peak flow meter

explanation: The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) is our trusty bedside tool for checking a patient's level of consciousness. You'll use this a lot in clinicals!

question: Why do we want a mix of different professions (multidisciplinary) on a QI team?

options.A: It is the only way to secure a larger operational budget
options.B: Patient care involves many different departments and professions
options.C: Hospital accreditation boards require equal staff representation
options.D: Single-discipline teams are legally prohibited in hospitals

explanation: That's right! Since healthcare touches pharmacy, lab, nursing, and medicine, fixing a process needs input from every department involved.

question: What happens during the acrosome reaction when a sperm reaches the outer layers of an egg?

options.A: Enzymes are released from the sperm head to digest a path through protective layers
options.B: The sperm tail falls off completely to anchor the head inside the follicle
options.C: The egg swallows the entire sperm tail without using any chemical help
options.D: Protective antibodies coat the sperm to prevent premature entry

explanation: Think of the acrosome as a tiny chemical drill at the tip of the sperm head, releasing special enzymes to clear a pathway through the egg's defenses.

question: What is the primary reason for initiating a patient referral to another facility?

options.A: The hospital building needs routine plumbing repairs
options.B: The patient's clinical needs exceed current facility resources
options.C: The attending doctor wants to take a short vacation
options.D: The patient complains about the food quality on the ward

explanation: Referrals are done when specialized care, advanced equipment, or specific expertise is required that the current health center cannot provide. [learn more](GNS112_U2_T5#GNS112_U2_T5_h4)

question: What is the main thing that separates a true experiment from a quasi-experiment?

options.A: Avoiding all forms of statistical testing
options.B: The use of patient interviews for data collection
options.C: The presence of a clinical nurse researcher
options.D: Random assignment of participants to groups

explanation: You nailed it! True experiments use random chance (like flipping a coin) to drop people into different groups, while quasi-experiments don't use strict random mixing. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T13#GNS217_U3_T13_h4)

question: What does Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR) tell us?

options.A: Total calories burned during a strenuous two-hour workout
options.B: Percentage of body fat compared to lean muscle mass
options.C: Maximum amount of food a person can digest in one day
options.D: Minimum calories needed to maintain basic life functions at rest

explanation: BMR is your body's resting engine speed—the bare minimum calories needed just to keep your organs ticking while you rest.

question: What post-procedure instruction should a nurse give to a patient who just received a knee injection?

options.A: Remove the sterile bandage right away and soak in mud
options.B: Run a long distance immediately to spread the medicine
options.C: Take off all clothes and stay in a hot sauna for hours
options.D: Rest the joint and apply ice packs to reduce swelling

explanation: Resting the joint and icing it helps prevent excess irritation and controls post-injection discomfort. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T9#GNS125_U3_T9_h7)

question: What is the physical shape of a DNA molecule?

options.A: A flat square sheet
options.B: A single circle
options.C: A branched tree structure
options.D: A double helix

explanation: DNA naturally twists into a spiral ladder shape referred to as a double helix. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T7#GNS111_U1_T7_h1)

question: Around what decade did psychotropic medications like chlorpromazine first become widely available?

options.A: The 1920s
options.B: The 1950s
options.C: The 1800s
options.D: The 1980s

explanation: The 1950s changed everything! The arrival of chlorpromazine and other drugs marked a massive turning point in how mental illness was treated medically.

question: Which substance is often given early to trap toxins in the stomach before they get into the bloodstream?

options.A: Activated charcoal
options.B: Syrup of ipecac
options.C: Magnesium citrate
options.D: Normal saline flush

explanation: Activated charcoal works like a magnet! It grabs onto many drugs and chemicals right in the gut so they can't get absorbed into the body.

question: Why is the community nurse so vital in settings with limited resources?

options.A: They replace the need for any secondary or tertiary healthcare facilities
options.B: They have unlimited access to advanced mechanical ventilators and dialysis machines
options.C: They serve as the first line of defense to stabilize rapidly deteriorating patients before hospital transfer
options.D: They are the only healthcare workers legally permitted to perform major surgeries

explanation: Spotting danger signs early and starting care right away makes all the difference when a patient arrives at a local clinic first.

question: Which antibody class is the main driver behind severe allergic reactions like anaphylaxis?

options.A: Immunoglobulin E
options.B: Immunoglobulin G
options.C: Immunoglobulin A
options.D: Immunoglobulin M

explanation: Think of IgE as the trigger-happy antibody! In anaphylaxis, IgE binds to mast cells and sets off a massive allergic chain reaction.

question: In the emergency ABCDE assessment check, what does the letter 'B' stand for?

options.A: Breathing
options.B: Blood pressure
options.C: Bone
options.D: Bleeding

explanation: Easy and correct! 'B' stands for Breathing. Checking chest movement is one of the very first things we do for any emergency patient.

question: What type of energy does an MRI machine use to create images of the body?

options.A: Ultraviolet light rays
options.B: High-frequency sound waves
options.C: High doses of ionizing radiation
options.D: Strong magnetic fields and radiofrequency waves

explanation: An MRI does not use harmful radiation like X-rays or CT scans; instead, it uses large magnets and radio waves to take pictures inside the body. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T12#GNS123_U2_T12_h1)

question: Why is it important to include family members in dietary education for a patient requiring a low salt diet?

options.A: Family members are the ones who administer oral medications at home
options.B: Family members are legally responsible for paying hospital medical bills
options.C: Family members must also follow the exact same medical diagnosis
options.D: Family members usually prepare the meals and must support the dietary changes

explanation: In many homes, cooking is shared or done by someone other than the patient, so family buy-in ensures the right food gets cooked. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T007#GNS227_U6_T007_h7)

question: Why is it wonderful for Nigerian nurses to recommend local soups like ugwu and egusi during nutrition talks?

options.A: They are affordable, culturally familiar, and rich in essential nutrients
options.B: They are the only foods allowed by traditional customs during pregnancy
options.C: They replace the need for antenatal clinic attendance
options.D: They completely eliminate the risk of gestational high blood pressure

explanation: Our local soups are packed with vitamins, iron, and good fats! They are easy to find, pocket-friendly, and nourishing.

question: A teenager avoids emergency contraception because she believes it causes permanent infertility. What type of barrier is this?

options.A: Economic restriction
options.B: Legal impediment
options.C: Psychosocial misconception
options.D: Physical limitation

explanation: Myths and false beliefs about side effects are psychological barriers rooted in misinformation. Gentle education goes a long way here.

question: What is the main chemical messenger the endocrine system uses to send signals around the body?

options.A: Electrolytes
options.B: Hormones
options.C: Neurotransmitters
options.D: Plasma proteins

explanation: Think of hormones as the body's internal mail system! Endocrine glands release them straight into the bloodstream to tell different organs what to do.

question: What is the medical name often used for andropause?

options.A: Late-onset hypogonadism
options.B: Primary hyperandrogenism
options.C: Chronic orchitis
options.D: Acute testicular failure

explanation: You'll often hear andropause called late-onset hypogonadism because it simply means a slow drop in male hormone levels as men grow older. Great job learning the clinical terms!

question: What is a major limitation of administrative controls compared to engineering controls?

options.A: They are completely invisible to workers and inspectors
options.B: They remove hazards completely from the physical workspace
options.C: They rely heavily on human behavior and can be forgotten or ignored
options.D: They cost more money than buying new factory buildings

explanation: Because administrative controls depend on people following rules and schedules, they fail more easily than automated engineering barriers. [learn more](GNS225_U7_T8#GNS225_U7_T8_h5)

question: According to Maslow's pyramid of human needs, which level comes absolutely first?

options.A: Esteem needs
options.B: Physiological needs
options.C: Safety needs
options.D: Self-actualization

explanation: That's right! Before anything else, our basic survival needs like food, water, and rest have to be sorted out.

question: Which lab results are most important for a nurse to check before starting a patient on anti-bleeding therapy?

options.A: Clotting profiles like PT, INR, and aPTT
options.B: Thyroid hormone panels
options.C: Fasting blood sugar levels
options.D: Routine liver enzymes only

explanation: Always check your patient's clotting baseline! Tests like PT, INR, and aPTT tell you how their blood is currently handling coagulation.

question: Why must people who already have a disease be left out of the denominator when calculating incidence?

options.A: They are usually transferred to a different clinic
options.B: They cannot develop a condition they already have
options.C: They skew the financial data of the health facility
options.D: They automatically increase the recovery rate statistics

explanation: Incidence tracks *new* infections. If someone already has the illness, they aren't at risk of catching it for the first time anymore!

question: Which of these is NOT a risk factor for getting Korsakoff syndrome?

options.A: Regular aerobic exercise
options.B: Hyperemesis gravidarum
options.C: Chronic alcohol abuse
options.D: Prolonged malnutrition

explanation: Exercise keeps you healthy! It doesn't cause vitamin shortages, unlike severe vomiting, poor diet, or heavy drinking.

question: What is the main difference between an impairment and a disability?

options.A: An impairment only affects children, while a disability only affects older adults.
options.B: An impairment is a bodily difference, while a disability is often created by environmental barriers.
options.C: An impairment is temporary, whereas a disability is always permanent.
options.D: A disability is purely psychological, while an impairment is strictly physical.

explanation: Impairment refers to the actual structure or function of the body, but the physical and social environment often turns that impairment into a functional disability. [learn more](GNS225_U5_T9#GNS225_U5_T9_h1)

question: What is the best immediate physical step to help reduce swelling right after a fresh injury?

options.A: Using a heating pad
options.B: Applying a cold pack
options.C: Placing a warm moist towel
options.D: Giving a deep tissue massage

explanation: Great clinical instinct! Cold constricts blood vessels, which slows down fluid pooling into the area and helps numb the sharp pain right away.

question: Which lab value usually climbs when a patient has failing kidneys and can't clear protein waste?

options.A: Serum potassium levels
options.B: Red blood cell count
options.C: Blood urea nitrogen
options.D: Total body water weight

explanation: Since urea is the main waste product of protein, sluggish kidneys mean urea backs up, causing Blood Urea Nitrogen (BUN) levels to rise.

question: What is the teach-back method used for during patient education?

options.A: Having the patient explain instructions in their own words
options.B: Reviewing textbook chapters with the family caregiver
options.C: Allowing the patient to teach nursing students clinical skills
options.D: Testing the patient's long-term memory after a stroke

explanation: The teach-back method requires patients to repeat back what they understood, confirming they actually grasped the instructions. [learn more](GNS324_U1_T7#GNS324_U1_T7_h5)

question: On day four, a new mother complains that her right calf is suddenly painful, swollen, and warm to the touch. What should pop into your head first?

options.A: Deep vein thrombosis
options.B: Uterine subinvolution
options.C: Postpartum blues
options.D: Normal postpartum fatigue

explanation: Pain and swelling in just one leg after childbirth is a classic warning sign of a blood clot (DVT). Always take this seriously and report it immediately!

question: Which of these is a dangerous medication habit that you should warn patients against?

options.A: Checking expiration dates on packaging before swallowing pills
options.B: Reporting any unusual itching or rashes to your healthcare provider
options.C: Sharing your leftover antibiotics with sick family members
options.D: Completing the entire dose prescribed by a qualified doctor

explanation: Never share your drugs! Dosage needs vary from person to person, and what cures your infection could harm someone else.

question: How does unmanaged chronic insomnia affect a patient's metabolism?

options.A: It accelerates muscle growth by boosting resting growth hormone production.
options.B: It impairs glucose tolerance and increases the risk of type 2 diabetes and obesity.
options.C: It causes rapid weight loss by burning excess calories during nocturnal awakenings.
options.D: It eliminates the body's need for dietary carbohydrates entirely.

explanation: Poor sleep messes with the hormones that control appetite and blood sugar, making it much easier to gain weight and harder for the body to handle glucose properly.

question: Why is a multidisciplinary team necessary for the comprehensive care of an FGM survivor?

options.A: Hospital regulations require at least three different doctors to sign off on treatment.
options.B: Insurance policies only cover care if multiple departments are billed.
options.C: The condition involves complex physical, surgical, and psychological needs that one discipline cannot solve alone.
options.D: Surgical repair is impossible without psychiatric clearance first.

explanation: Holistic recovery requires medical treatment for physical ailments alongside psychological support for emotional trauma. [learn more](GNS312_U1_T6#GNS312_U1_T6_h7)

question: What is the very first thing you check when a patient arrives with an acute sting?

options.A: Applying a cold ice pack to reduce swelling
options.B: Assessing airway, breathing, and circulation
options.C: Inquiring about past medical history
options.D: Cleaning the wound with soap and water

explanation: Always ABCs first! Checking airway, breathing, and circulation helps you catch severe allergic reactions or shock before they get out of hand.

question: Which type of isolation is used to protect a patient with a very weak immune system?

options.A: Strict contact isolation
options.B: Respiratory isolation
options.C: Protective isolation
options.D: Standard isolation

explanation: Protective or reverse isolation guards patients who cannot fight off everyday germs by keeping outside microorganisms away from them. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T16#GNS122_U2_T16_h3)

question: For a mother who had a safe, normal delivery, when should her very first post-natal check happen?

options.A: Exactly on the fourteenth day
options.B: Within 24 hours of birth
options.C: After six months
options.D: At the end of the second week

explanation: That first check within 24 hours is super important to catch immediate issues like heavy bleeding or shock before they become emergencies.

question: Why are pupil checks an essential part of the emergency neurological evaluation?

options.A: Pupil reactions tell the nurse the exact blood glucose level
options.B: They are used to measure the patient's daily fluid intake needs
options.C: They show whether the patient has an allergy to bright hospital lights
options.D: Unequal or sluggish pupils can indicate increased pressure inside the brain

explanation: Changes in pupil size and light reflex often reflect brainstem compression or intracranial pathology, serving as an early warning sign. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T8#GNS112_U7_T8_h6)
